How to read this report

Every number on this page is one of four kinds, and each is tagged where it appears.

  • filed A figure stated in the S-1, extracted by pattern-matching with the sentence that states it and its page.
  • derived Arithmetic on filed figures: ratios, sums, bounds.
  • assumption A modeling choice where the filing is silent. Each is listed with its reason in Appendix B and most can be changed in section 3.
  • Jev A judgment that needs reading: which theme a passage supports, how an agreement can be cancelled, which role a counterparty plays. Jev returns these as typed answers with probabilities (section 5).

Click any chart element or table row to open its source in a side panel: the quoted sentence, the clause, or every passage that was counted. Part I answers four economic questions; Part II shows how the filing distributes its emphasis, and how Jev was used to measure it.

Part I The economics
1

Gross margin

What does it cost to produce what Anthropic sells?

The question

How much of each revenue dollar is left after the cost of producing it, when that cost includes the compute used to train the models being sold, not only the compute used to serve them?

Why it matters

Software companies are valued on gross margin. Anthropic's accounting gross margin counts only serving compute, while most of its compute goes to training, research and internal use, which sit in R&D. Where you draw the line decides whether this looks like a software business or an infrastructure business.

How to read it

The waterfall walks H1 2026 revenue down to operating income using the filing's expenses by function (Note 8). Bars are tagged as filed, a floor, or a bucket the filing does not split. The chart to the right charges a growing share of non-serving compute against revenue; the shaded band is the range the filing allows.

Bridge to operating income

Key takeaway

Accounting gross margin (85.4%) is a serving margin, not a measure of what it costs to produce the product. Counting all compute as cost of goods gives 45.1%. After channel fees the figure is about 28%. The truth for current-period economics lies between, depending on how much of the $5.7B–$6.8B of non-serving compute you treat as the cost of today's models. FY2025 shows how fast this moved: its accounting gross margin was 39.5% and its operating margin -175.8%, including the $1.5B settlement.

2

Compute efficiency

How much of the growth was bought with compute, and is efficiency compounding?

The question

Is revenue growing faster than compute spending, and is that gap widening quarter after quarter?

Why it matters

If each new compute dollar earns more revenue than the last, the contracts in section 3 get easier to carry. If the improvement came in one-off steps, the contracts depend on the next step arriving.

How to read it

Bars are quarterly revenue and compute expense; the line is revenue per compute dollar, switchable between same-quarter, rolling, lagged (compute is contracted 12–18 months ahead and expensed as it arrives) and incremental views. Triangles mark model releases. The right chart splits each quarter's revenue growth into growth in compute and growth in revenue per compute dollar. That split is arithmetic, not cause and effect.

Revenue per compute dollar

Key takeaway

Efficiency improved sharply: revenue per compute dollar rose 3.67× year on year. But it has not compounded smoothly. The quarterly gain went from 19% to 3%, then jumped 102% after Opus 4.5. The incremental return fell from 6.09 to 3.14 revenue dollars per added compute dollar. Read the next releases as the test of whether the step pattern continues.

3

Contracted compute

What revenue and demand do the compute contracts require?

The question

Anthropic has signed compute and data-center agreements worth hundreds of billions of dollars, most payable whether or not the capacity is used. How much revenue, and how much demand growth, does it take for those contracts to pay for themselves?

Why it matters

These obligations are the largest numbers in the filing, larger than its cash, its equity raised and its revenue run-rate combined. They are the company's real leverage, even with almost no debt.

How to read it

Five steps. 3.1 reconciles the commitments into one ledger. 3.2 lays out when they are paid. 3.3 sets the discount rates. 3.4 values the contracts and solves for the demand growth they need, with live controls. 3.5 stresses the result.

3.1 Reconciled ledger

Commitments come from different notes and dates: purchase commitments at June 30 (Note 13), leases already running and leases not yet started (Note 7), and agreements signed after June 30 (Note 17). Named agreements are mapped into those categories, and estimates the filing excludes are kept apart. The result is a range, not a single number. Firm commitments are about $682B, the base case for everything below. The upper bound of $855B adds SpaceXAI after its notice period and the Nscale and Lambda deals that depend on those vendors' financing. The filing leaves its own total blank, and amendments signed after June 30 may restate amounts already counted, so the upper bound is a ceiling.

Cross-check: press reports, not the filing

Reporting on draft prospectuses before the public filing put the figure at more than $600B, or up to about $750B including deals still under negotiation: Bloomberg, October 20, 2026 (citing The Wall Street Journal: a draft prospectus put possible computing spend at up to $750B, including deals still under negotiation) · The Next Web, October 21, 2026 (summarizing the WSJ and Axios: more than $600B of future infrastructure costs, plus about $150B in deals under negotiation). The firm figure sits inside that range.

3.2 Payment calendar

Scope
Payment ramp-in from each agreement's start

3.3 Discount rates

The payments are owed whatever happens, so they are debt-like and discounted at Anthropic's own borrowing rate, which the filing discloses for its leases. Revenue, net of variable costs and tax, carries the business risk and is discounted at an unlevered cost of capital built from listed peers. One equity rate for both sides would shrink the payments too much and flatter the result.

3.4 Reverse DCF

Each year, the non-serving share of compute (training, research, internal use) is set aside and the rest is serving capacity. Revenue is the lower of two things. One is capacity × utilization × revenue per used serving dollar, calibrated to H1 2026 with usage-policy revenue removed. The other is demand, if a demand path is switched on. Non-compute operating costs and tax are subtracted; the result is discounted at the revenue rate and the payments at the payment rate. The model solves for the demand growth, and for the price-efficiency, at which NPV reaches zero.

3.5 Stress tests

Utilization scenarios at the current settings

Utilization is absolute only under the H1 2026 level set above; the relative column does not depend on it. Revenue in this model scales with utilization × price-efficiency, so high utilization at too low a price still fails. The demand columns show the growth each scenario needs.

Key takeaway

Capacity is not the constraint; demand is. The firm commitments, about $682B, need revenue to compound about 44% a year from today's run-rate to earn the discount rate, and the liquidity covenant holds from about 31%. If every contracted deal runs, up to $855B, the bar rises to about 69% a year. If demand instead filled all the firm capacity at H1 2026 revenue per serving dollar, the contracts would be worth $216B. The utilization needed depends on an assumed H1 2026 level and is shown relative to it.

4

Customer concentration

How concentrated is the revenue that has to carry these commitments?

The question

How much revenue depends on a small number of large customers, and is that dependence rising or falling?

Why it matters

Section 3 needs revenue to compound for years. Revenue concentrated in a few accounts can move quickly in either direction, and the largest AI customers can build or buy their own models.

How to read it

Counts of customers by annual spend (log scale), the growth and revenue share of $100K+ customers, and the top five's share of revenue. Click any bar or point for its source. The filing does not report revenue by spend band or name any customer.

Revenue quality notes from the filing

  • 5–7% of revenue in the nine months to Sep 30, 2026 came from customers later found violating usage policy or commercial terms. The company expects this to fall after stepped-up enforcement in August and September 2026. The model removes the midpoint.
  • Over 80% of Q3 2026 revenue came from model versions released in the prior six months. Revenue follows the release cycle.
  • 80% of H1 2026 revenue was consumption-based, which can fall as fast as it rises.
  • No single customer exceeded 10% of revenue in the nine months to Sep 30, 2026.
Key takeaway

The revenue base broadened through 2026. The top five's share fell from 36% to 21% while each top-five customer still set a record. Spending is concentrated: 74% of H1 2026 revenue came from $100K+ customers. The filing gives counts by spend band but not revenue by band, so it does not show how much of revenue the largest 250 hold, or whether they stay. The filing names no customer. A loss of the largest accounts is best treated as a stress, which section 3 runs.

Part II What the filing emphasizes
5

How Jev read the filing

Reading 300 pages at the level of individual passages, with a probability on every judgment

What Jev is. Jev is TypeSafe's System One model. It does not write text. It answers a question about a piece of text with a typed result: one option from a defined list, a yes/no probability, or a position on a described scale. Each result carries a probability. That makes reading behave like a function call, so code can threshold, rank, aggregate and re-run judgments the way it handles any other data.

Why use it here. Questions such as "does this passage state a concrete fact about compute commitments" or "can this agreement be cancelled, and how" need reading, not pattern-matching. They had to be asked of every passage, not a sample: 13,026 judgments at a median 90 ms per request, for $0.11 in total. Because every answer has a probability, every count on this page can be re-thresholded, and every judgment can be traced to the passage it was made on.

What it did not do. Jev did not produce any number in Part I. Figures were extracted by pattern-matching with their quotes, and all arithmetic is code. Jev typed the agreements and instruments that section 3 builds on, and the cross-check below shows those readings line up with the ledger.

  2. 2Typed questions to Jev Choice, Score and yes/no questions with plain-language criteria
  3. 3Policy in code Thresholds, shares, indexes, verdicts that must hold under two evidence bases
  4. 4Checks A second pass for stability, regex agreement, 21 of 21 author-read checks agreed

6

Words against facts

Does the filing spend its risk-factor words where its facts are?

The question

For each risk theme, is the share of risk-factor words in line with the share of concrete facts the rest of the filing carries about it?

Why it matters

Risk factors are written by counsel and cover everything. Comparing their emphasis with the document's own evidence shows which risks are asserted at length and which are documented but under-discussed.

How to read it

Each bubble is a theme. Above the dashed line, the theme gets more words than facts; below it, more facts than words. Colour is the verdict that holds whether or not the share-class and accounting sections count as evidence; grey themes depend on that choice. Click a bubble for its factors.

Key takeaway

The filing spends most of its risk-factor words on competition, AI safety and misuse, regulation, IP litigation, and cybersecurity and privacy, more than the rest of the document documents. It spends the least, relative to the facts it carries, on access to capital, supplier conflicts of interest, and talent. That is the opposite of where Part I finds the economic exposure. Six themes (compute supply, compute commitments, revenue and customers, model execution, governance, and share ownership and market) change verdict when the share-class and accounting sections are excluded, so only the agreements are called findings.

7

Where the evidence sits

Which sections of the filing carry the facts behind each theme?

The question

In which sections of the filing does Jev find concrete facts for each risk theme?

Why it matters

It shows where to read for each risk, and why the index in section 6 is reported on two evidence bases.

How to read it

Rows are themes, columns are sections. Switch between counts, each theme's distribution across sections, and the mean probability (which needs no threshold). Click a cell to read every passage counted.

Key takeaway

Most of the filing's facts sit in the Financial Statements (29% of counted passages) and MD&A (23%). Capital access, governance and stock themes draw heavily on the financial statements and capital-stock sections, which is why the index is reported with and without them.

8

The 88 risk factors

Every risk factor, sized by length and shaded by how specific it is

The question

Which risk factors are long, and which say something specific to Anthropic rather than generic language?

Why it matters

Length is not importance, but long and specific factors are where the company chose to disclose detail.

How to read it

Area is word count; shade is Jev's specificity score from 0 (generic) to 3 (Anthropic figures, dates and counterparties). Click a theme to zoom, then a factor to read it in full.

Key takeaway

Two thirds of the risk-factor words (67%) sit in factors that describe something that has already happened: the settlement, compute shortfalls, conflicts, export restrictions. The average factor scores 1.17 on a 0–3 specificity scale. The most specific factors are about government sales, data collection, safety commitments and compute commitments.

9

Industry boilerplate

How much of the risk section any AI-infrastructure issuer would write

The question

Which risk factors have a near-twin in a comparable filing?

Why it matters

Shared language is genre, not signal. What only Anthropic says is where its disclosure carries information.

How to read it

Jev matched each Anthropic heading against the ten closest headings in CoreWeave's March 2025 S-1. Grey is words in factors with a match; blue is words in factors without one.

Key takeaway

About 67% of risk-factor words sit in factors with a near-twin in CoreWeave's S-1 from March 2025. The least shared themes, supplier conflicts of interest, AI safety and misuse, and governance, are where Anthropic's disclosure is its own.

11

Counterparty roles

Who is investor, supplier, customer and competitor at once

The question

Which roles does each major counterparty hold toward Anthropic, according to the filing's own text?

Why it matters

The same companies supply the compute, finance it, buy from Anthropic and compete with it. The filing gives this one risk factor; the text documents it in many places.

How to read it

Shade is the strongest probability any passage reached for that role; the number is how many passages reached 0.8. Switch to mean probability or counts. Click a cell to read every passage, ranked.

Key takeaway

Amazon holds 6 and Google 6 of the seven roles at p ≥ 0.8: each is an investor, a financing source, a supplier, a customer, a distribution channel and a competitor. The filing mentions SpaceXAI, Nscale, and Lambda in only a few passages, so their roles rest on little text.

Appendix

A Method and limitations

  1. Payment dollars stand in for capacity. The filing gives no physical units (chips, megawatts), so a dollar of compute payment is treated as a dollar of capacity. The model cannot tell new capacity from prepayment or higher prices.
  2. Utilization is identified only relative to H1 2026. The filing shows revenue per serving-compute dollar, not how full the capacity was. Absolute utilization figures assume H1 2026 ran at the level set in the assumptions; the relative figure does not depend on it.
  3. The ledger's categories come from different notes and dates, which does not rule out overlap. Amendments after June 30 may restate amounts already in the June 30 figure. The firm subtotal removes the cancelable and vendor-conditional agreements that can be identified; other amounts 'subject to contractual conditions' cannot be separated.
  4. The payment calendar is shaped by assumptions where the filing is silent: the filing leaves its own aggregate and near-term commitment figures blank. Windows come from the filing where stated; ramp-in and residual spreads are assumptions.
  5. Cash is modeled annually, so a covenant breach inside a year can be missed. Working capital, capital expenditure beyond the leases, interest income, stock compensation (a real cost to shareholders through dilution) and any value after the contracts end are excluded.
  6. Demand growth is a single constant rate from the Q2 2026 run-rate. Revenue is the lower of demand and capacity, so growth beyond capacity adds nothing.
  7. Discount rates are modeled, not externally validated. Peer selection, the treatment of leases as debt-like, and the cash-flow definitions involve judgment. The equity risk premium has no as-of date in its source.
  8. Jev's probabilities describe its answer distribution, not measured accuracy. Thresholds were chosen, not tuned against labels; the author-read checks and the regex agreements are the validation shown.

Sources

Primary filing

Anthropic, PBC, Form S-1 registration statement, filed with the SEC on October 26, 2026. CIK 2130357, accession no. 0001628280-26-067168.

  • S-1 document
  • Filing index, with exhibits
  • Anthropic, PBC on EDGAR

Every figure, quote and passage in this report comes from this filing.

Comparison filing

CoreWeave, Inc., Form S-1 registration statement, filed with the SEC on March 3, 2025. CIK 1769628, accession no. 0001193125-25-044231.

  • S-1 document
  • Filing index

Its risk-factor headings are the comparison set in section 9.

Market data for the discount rates

  • 10-year US Treasury yield, 5.00% on October 23, 2026: US Treasury daily par yield curve
  • US equity risk premium, 4.46%: market-risk-premium country table (undated in source)
  • Peer betas, market capitalizations and debt for Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Oracle, Palantir, Snowflake, ServiceNow, Datadog, CoreWeave: company profiles and balance sheets

Retrieved through Financial Modeling Prep. The payment-side rate uses the S-1's own lease rate (Note 7). See section 3.3.

Press reports used as a cross-check

  • Bloomberg, October 20, 2026: citing The Wall Street Journal: a draft prospectus put possible computing spend at up to $750B, including deals still under negotiation
  • The Next Web, October 21, 2026: summarizing the WSJ and Axios: more than $600B of future infrastructure costs, plus about $150B in deals under negotiation

These describe draft prospectuses and are compared with the ledger in section 3.1. No figure in the model comes from them.

Reading judgments

TypeSafe's Jev: risk-factor typing, evidence, peer matching, agreements and counterparty roles. See section 5.
